# What Is IML? {background-color="#40666e"}

## Motivation

> "if the users do not trust a model or a prediction, they will not use it." @ribeiro2016Why [p. 1]

## Global and Local Foci

-   Global interpretability refers to the totality of a population.

-   Local interpretability concerns prediction in a specific instance.

## Different Approaches

-   DALEX [@biecek2018DALEX]

-   IML = Interpretable Machine Learning [@molnar2018Iml]

-   LIME = Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations [@ribeiro2016Why]

# Partial Dependence Plots {background-color="#40666e"}

## What Is a Partial Dependence Plot?

-   A partial dependence plot (PDP) visualizes the relationship between a specific feature and a target, while averaging out the effects of the remaining features.

-   This is based on a consideration of all training or test instances.

## How Is the PDP Constructed?

1.  Let $f(.)$ be the function that we trained.

2.  Choose $X_j$ as the feature of interest. Create a grid of values ${\cal G} = \{ g_1, g_2, \cdots, g_m \}$ spanning the range of $X_j$.

## How Is the PDP Constructed? Cont'd

3.  For each $g \in {\cal G}$,

    1.  Replace the $j$th feature in all instances with $g$; call the remaining features $\boldsymbol{x}_i^*$.

    2.  Predict the outcome using the modified data: $\hat{y}_i^{(j)} = f(x_{ij} = g, \boldsymbol{x}_i^*)$.

    3.  Average the predictions over all instances:

        $$
        \hat{f}_j = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i^{(j)}
        $$

    4.  Plot the results.

## The Boston Housing Prices Once More

::: panel-tabset
## Comment

-   We fit a random forest to the Boston Housing data.

-   This produces $R$ trees that are aggregated.

-   This aggregate is not so easily interpretable.

## Data

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(mlbench)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
tidymodels_prefer()
data("BostonHousing2")
df <- BostonHousing2 %>%
  mutate(chas = as.numeric(chas) - 1) %>%
  select(-town, -tract, -lon, -lat, -medv)
set.seed(10)
housing_split <- initial_split(df, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(housing_split)
test <- testing(housing_split)
```

## Flow

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(bonsai)
rf_recipe <- recipe(cmedv ~ ., data = train)
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(),
                       trees = 100,
                       min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_mode("regression") %>%
  set_engine("partykit")
initial_flow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

```

## Tuning

```{r}
#| echo: true
rf_para <- extract_parameter_set_dials(rf_spec) %>%
  finalize(train)
set.seed(20)
rf_grid <- grid_latin_hypercube(rf_para,
                                size = 25,
                                variogram_range = 0.75,
                                original = TRUE)
set.seed(30)
cv_folds <- vfold_cv(train, v = 10)
rf_metrics <- metric_set(rsq)
doParallel::registerDoParallel()
rf_tune <- initial_flow %>%
  tune_grid(cv_folds, grid = rf_grid, metrics = rf_metrics)
rf_best <- select_best(rf_tune)
```

## Final

```{r}
#| echo: true
rf_updated <- finalize_model(rf_spec,
                             rf_best)
workflow_new <- initial_flow %>%
  update_model(rf_updated)
rf_fit_final <- workflow_new %>%
  fit(data = train)
```
:::

## Explainer

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
library(DALEXtra)
housing_explainer <- explain_tidymodels(
  model = rf_fit_final,
  data = test,
  y = test$cmedv
)
```

## PDP Syntax

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
pdp_nox <- model_profile(
  housing_explainer,
  variables = "nox",
  N = NULL
)
as_tibble(pdp_nox$agr_profiles) %>%
  ggplot(aes(`_x_`, `_yhat_`)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_rug(sides = "b") +
  labs(
    x = "Pollution",
    y = "Predicted Median Housing Price",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

# Breakdown Plots {background-color="#40666e"}

## What Is a Breakdown Plot?

-   A breakdown plot breaks a prediction down into contributions of individual features.

-   It does so

    -   Following an additive logic

    -   Taking sequencing into account

## Creating a Breakdown Plot

1.  Create a baseline prediction:

    $$
    \phi_i^0 = \mathbb{E}[f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)]
    $$

2.  Incremental contributions:

    -   Consider a sequence $q$ that orders the features in terms of being added 1st, 2nd, etc.

    -   Let $S$ denote the set of features that have been considered prior to $X_j$.

    -   Then

        $$
        \phi_j^q = f(S \cup \{j\}) - f(S)
        $$

## Creating a Breakdown Plot Cont'd

3.  Consider all $Q$ permutations of orderings of features. Then the average contribution across orderings is

    $$
    \phi_j = \frac{1}{Q} \sum_{q=1}^Q \phi_j^q
    $$

4.  Plot these averages in a bar chart.

# Shapley Values {background-color="#40666e"}

## A New Approach to Understanding Feature Importance

-   Proposed by @lundberg2017Unified and based on cooperative game theory [@shapley1953Value].

-   Looks at the contribution of a feature depending on the order in which it was added to the model.

-   We create $R$ random orderings and assess

    -   Mean contribution

    -   Range of contributions

-   This can be done locally or globally.

## Local Shap-Values

::: panel-tabset
## Selection

```{r}
#| echo: true
# We select (for instance) the 100th test sample
temp2 <- test[100,]
temp2
```

## Shapley

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(1802)
shap100 <- 
  predict_parts(
    explainer = housing_explainer, 
    new_observation = temp2, 
    type = "shap",
    B = 20
  )
```

## Plot1

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(forcats)
shap100 %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(mean_val = mean(contribution)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(variable = fct_reorder(variable, abs(mean_val))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(contribution, variable, fill = mean_val > 0)) +
  geom_col(data = ~distinct(., variable, mean_val), 
           aes(mean_val, variable), 
           alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5) +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(y = NULL) +
  theme_bw()
```

## Plot2

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(forcats)
shap100 %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(mean_val = mean(contribution)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%

  ggplot(aes(contribution, variable, fill = mean_val > 0)) +
  geom_col(data = ~distinct(., variable, mean_val),

           alpha = 0.5) +

```
